title: Vendor ML pipeline threat model & evidence checklist
content:
Purpose: This checklist is intended to help Redwood assess ML vendor/core-inference pipeline security and operational risk. It focuses on the full pipeline (ingest, training/finetune, model artifact handling, inference/runtime, telemetry) and specifies evidence artifacts we typically request during procurement or annual reassessments. Use as a supplement to the standard vendor security questionnaire; this is ML-specific and prioritized for production inference vendors, managed model hosts, or partners that run training/finetune workflows.

Scope & assumptions:
- Applies to vendors that: host models, accept customer prompts or datasets, perform training/finetuning, or run hosted inference for Redwood customers.
- Does not replace legal DPA or SOC/ISO reports; it identifies ML-specific gaps and evidence items to request.
- Risk tolerance: medium (we require remediation of high-risk items before onboarding for regulated customers).

How to use:
- Walk vendor through each section. Mark evidence provided and ask for clarifications on any items marked "partial" or "no".
- Use scoring rubric (Acceptable / Needs Clarification / High Risk) in procurement notes.

Section A — Data flows and boundaries (High priority)
1) Dataflow diagram: vendor provides end-to-end diagram showing all ingress, storage, processing, egress points, and subprocessors. Evidence: diagram file (PNG/PDF) + short narrative.
2) PII classification: vendor documents how incoming data is classified and segmented (automated tagging, user labels). Evidence: classification policy excerpt.
3) Inference telemetry retention: demonstrate retention windows for raw prompts, model outputs, logs, and KV-cache. Evidence: retention config, retention schedule.
4) Data residency controls: where is customer data stored/processed? Evidence: region list, account separation design.

Section B — Model artifacts & weights supply chain (High priority)
1) Model provenance: source of model weights used in production (public repo, licensed weights, proprietary). Evidence: license/docs and hash/signature of artifact.
2) Model integrity validation: processes to validate downloaded weights (checksums, signatures, notarization). Evidence: checksum policy + sample signed manifest.
3) Component provenance for third-party libraries and compiled kernels. Evidence: SBOM or dependency manifest for serving stack.

Section C — Training/finetuning and dataset handling (Medium priority)
1) Data minimization for finetune jobs: controls to avoid retention of raw customer datasets after tuning complete. Evidence: retention policy and deletion confirmation process.
2) Isolation of training jobs: multi-tenant isolation details, ephemeral cluster cleanup, snapshot handling. Evidence: runbook or design doc.
3) Opportunity for leakage via caching: how are dataset-derived prefixes handled in caches? Evidence: cache eviction design and any masking heuristics.

Section D — Serving runtime security (High priority)
1) Access control: RBAC for model deployment, ability to restrict who can push model weights to prod. Evidence: screenshots/policy names from IAM console + approval workflow description.
2) KV cache and prompt caching: encryption-at-rest and per-tenant or per-customer namespace enforcement. Evidence: config snippets + encryption scheme.
3) Sandbox for tool-calling / function calls: isolation between user-executed tools and the control plane. Evidence: architecture diagram + sandboxing tech used.
4) Rate limiting and abuse mitigation: per-tenant throttles, anomaly detection for prompt floods. Evidence: policy thresholds and sample alerts.

Section E — Secrets, key management & cryptography (High priority)
1) KMS/HSM usage: whether model keys or customer material is protected by KMS/HSM and rotated. Evidence: KMS account config + rotation cadence.
2) Secrets in CI/CD: how model signing keys and deployment tokens are protected in build pipelines. Evidence: CI policy + sample masking logs.

Section F — Observability, explainability & tamper detection (Medium priority)
1) Telemetry necessary for incident triage: request list (models, runtimes, request ids, truncated prompt/response hashes). Evidence: telemetry catalog export.
2) Tamper detection for model artifacts: attestations or immutable storage for canonical models. Evidence: attestation logs or immutability configuration.

Section G — Operational resilience & degraded modes (Medium priority)
1) Graceful fallback policies: default route when a model fails (smaller model, cached responses, degrade-to-read-only). Evidence: routing policy examples.
2) Backups and rollback: how are model versions rolled back and backups retained? Evidence: backup schedule + sample rollback runbook.

Section H — Incident response & forensics (High priority)
1) Incident timeline and customer notification: SLAs for notification and content of initial report. Evidence: incident notification template.
2) Forensic evidence preservation: how long raw prompts and system logs can be preserved on request for investigations. Evidence: preservation runbook.

Section I — Privacy-preserving controls & regulatory flags (High priority for regulated customers)
1) Differential privacy / pseudonymization options for training. Evidence: technical design notes or library usage.
2) Right-to-be-forgotten support: process to remove a customer data record across all stores and model artifacts. Evidence: deletion flow and verification sample.

Section J — Testing, evals and quality guards (Medium priority)
1) Regression detection: how are new model deployments evaluated against baseline prompt sets? Evidence: evaluation harness outputs and threshold definitions.
2) Red-team / adversarial testing for prompt injection or model hallucination vectors. Evidence: red-team reports or summary.

Evidence request matrix (what to ask for immediately)
- Mandatory (must provide before production onboarding): dataflow diagram, model provenance manifest (hash/signature), KMS ownership/rotation policy, IAM roles for model deploy, incident notification template.
- Strongly encouraged (provide in parallel or prior to contract signature): SBOM, telemetry catalog extract, backup/rollback runbook, privacy deletion proof-of-concept.
- Optional (nice to have): red-team summary, DP/PP algorithm description, fine-grain telemetry retention controls.

Scoring rubric (quick):
- Acceptable: Evidence provided and matches claims; no unresolved concerns.
- Needs Clarification: Evidence partial or missing minor details; vendor to respond in 5 business days.
- High Risk: Missing mandatory evidence or negative architecture (e.g., single-tenant keys shared across customers). Remediate before production.

Red flags (escalate to legal/infosec):
- Vendor cannot produce model artifact checksums or provenance for models in production.
- Vendor stores raw prompts indefinitely and has no deletion workflow.
- Model signing/deployment keys are shared in plaintext in CI logs or repo.
- No documented isolation between tenants for training jobs.

Sample vendor response template (ask vendor to complete):
- Dataflow diagram: [link]
- Model provenance: [type/source] + [artifact hash/signature]
- KMS/HSM: [provider] + [rotation cadence] + [who has key admin rights]
- RBAC for deployment: [description] + [links to IAM policies]
- Incident notification: [SLA hours] + [primary contact]
- Items pending: [list with dates]\n
Contract clause suggestions (to hand to legal):
- Artifact provenance warranty: vendor warrants that all model weights provided to Redwood are accompanied by a verifiable checksum and a licensing provenance statement.
- Ephemeral telemetry retention clause: vendor agrees to retain raw prompts only for X days (configurable by customer) unless longer retention is required by law or with explicit customer consent.
- Model rollback and forensics cooperation: vendor will preserve relevant model versions and telemetry for at least 90 days following an incident and will cooperate with Redwood for forensic analysis.
- Subprocessor binding: vendor must impose equivalent ML-specific obligations on subprocessors handling model weights, finetune datasets, or serving telemetry.

Notes & next steps for assessor:
- Prioritize evidence marked mandatory; escalate any High Risk items to InfoSec and Procurement.
- If vendor provides SOC/ISO reports, use them to cross-check controls but always require ML-specific artefacts above.
- Template can be shortened to a one-pager for low-risk vendors (e.g., SaaS that only proxies inference and never stores prompts).

Appendix A — Minimal example evidence checklist (one-pager extract)
- Diagram: yes/no
- Model hash: yes/no
- KMS used: yes/no
- Retention days (prompts): number
- RBAC enforced: yes/no
- Incident SLA (hours): number
- Red-team report available: yes/no

Appendix B — Common mitigations to suggest to vendors (quick list)
- Adopt signed artifact manifests and publish checksums to an immutable store.
- Implement tenant-scoped KV caches with automatic prefix-scrubbing.
- Shorten default telemetry retention and offer per-customer configs.
- Introduce automated regression gates in deployment pipelines tied to eval prompts.

This document is intentionally pragmatic and vendor-oriented; update with vendor-specific follow-ups and attach evidence files to the procurement ticket (JIRA-RISK-1193).
